summaries.example: Imagine you are sure that your backpack is in your classroom because you just saw it there. Then a teacher tells you the room was cleaned and your backpack was moved. You may stop believing it is still there. Feeling very sure is one kind of certainty, but a belief can still change when new evidence appears.
summaries.summary: Certainty is a special way of talking about beliefs. A person may feel completely sure, but that feeling is not automatically the same as having the best possible reasons. Philosophers usually focus on epistemic certainty: certainty connected with truth, evidence, and justification. They have proposed different ideas about it. Perhaps a certain belief cannot be doubted, cannot be false, has the highest possible support, or cannot be weakened by new evidence. Each idea faces problems. For example, someone might be unable to doubt a belief because of fear or habit rather than good reasons. A belief that is true by definition might also be believed for a silly reason, so truth alone may not make it certain. The entry also separates certainty at one time from certainty that remains stable over time. Finally, it asks how certainty helps with reasoning, speaking, and practical choices. The main lesson is that certainty is an important goal, but its exact meaning is difficult and debated.
key_ideas: Certainty is about how well a belief is supported, not only about how strongly someone feels.
Philosophers have suggested several ways to understand certainty: a belief might be impossible to doubt, impossible to be wrong, supported as well as possible, or protected from defeating evidence.
Certainty can concern one moment, or it can mean that a belief stays secure as part of a larger group of beliefs.
Some philosophers think certainty is needed for knowledge, while others think we can have useful knowledge that is less than certain.
Certainty can help us reason and decide, but people disagree about whether we need certainty before speaking or acting.
summaries.why_it_matters: We often need to decide whether a reason is strong enough to trust. Thinking about certainty helps us separate “I feel sure” from “I have excellent reasons.” It also helps us understand why people can disagree about knowledge, evidence, and doubt while still trying to think carefully.

important_terms.definition: A belief held with the strongest possible support or status. Philosophers disagree about exactly what makes a belief certain.
Feeling completely sure that something is true. This feeling can be strong even when the belief is not well supported.
A serious doubt or argument that gives us a reason to question a belief.
The idea that a belief cannot be wrong or false.
The idea that a belief cannot be defeated by any good new reason or evidence.

questions_to_think_about: Can you feel sure about something and still be wrong?
Is a belief more trustworthy because you cannot imagine doubting it?
Should you wait for complete certainty before making an everyday decision?
Can a belief be certain now but become doubtful later?

summaries.example: Suppose a student sees a distant bird and believes it is a hawk. The visual evidence may make the belief reasonable, but similar-looking birds could provide a defeater—a fact that lowers the belief’s support. An account of certainty based only on the student’s confidence might call the belief certain too quickly. An account based on indefeasibility must explain why possible defeating evidence is excluded, and an account based on infallibility must explain in what sense the belief could not have been false. The example shows why certainty is stronger and harder to analyze than ordinary justified knowledge.
summaries.summary: The entry examines certainty as an epistemic status of beliefs and explains why it is difficult to analyze without controversy. Psychological certainty is maximal conviction; epistemic certainty concerns the highest level of epistemic standing. These can coincide, but they need not: a person may lack full confidence in a belief that nevertheless has the best possible epistemic status, or may be completely confident for poor reasons. The entry concentrates on four conceptions of epistemic certainty. Indubitability treats certainty as resistance to doubt, but resistance may result from irrational commitment, and even well-supported beliefs can sometimes be reasonably questioned. Infallibility treats certainty as the impossibility of error, yet it must identify the relevant modality and avoid making every belief in a necessary truth automatically certain. Inimitability understands certainty as maximal justification, but “maximal” can be relative to a person or an unfortunate epistemic situation. Indefeasibility requires protection from relevant defeating propositions, but it is unclear how one belief reduces another’s warrant and how external removal of defeaters would improve a weak basis. The entry then distinguishes certainty at a moment from certainty over time within a coherent system. It concludes by considering certainty’s proposed roles in inference, assertion, and practical reasoning, including contextualist views that allow standards to vary. No account is presented as completely satisfactory.
key_ideas: Certainty is an epistemic property of beliefs, but it is not straightforwardly identical with knowledge; many philosophers allow fallible knowledge that is less than certain.
The major conceptions considered are indubitability, infallibility, inimitability, and indefeasibility. Each captures an intuitive feature of certainty but encounters objections.

Indubitability can describe psychological inability to doubt without explaining why the belief deserves that status. If good reasons explain the inability, those reasons—not mere indubitability—seem fundamental.

Infallibility must specify the relevant sense in which a belief could not be false. Logical or metaphysical necessity is too strong for some paradigmatic certainties, while justification-based accounts risk regress problems.
Certainty has both a temporal dimension and a structural dimension: a belief may be secure while entertained, yet not remain secure when separated from a wider system of beliefs.

Applications include using certainties as premises, assessing whether certainty is required for assertion, and asking whether practical reasoning may legitimately rely on highly probable but uncertain claims.
summaries.why_it_matters: Certainty is a useful test case for understanding evidence, knowledge, doubt, and rational action. It shows that a belief can be true, justified, confidently held, or stable without these features automatically being identical. The debate also clarifies a practical tension: demanding certainty may protect us from error, but treating certainty as rare may make ordinary reasoning and communication seem irrational. Philosophical analysis helps identify exactly which standard a situation requires.

important_terms.definition: A property of a belief concerning its epistemic standing: roughly, having the highest possible status of justification or warrant.
Certainty understood as maximal conviction or confidence in a belief. It may come apart from the belief’s epistemic quality.
A position or argument claiming that our beliefs fall short of knowledge or certainty, often because doubt can be raised about them.
The view that certainty involves a belief’s being unable to be false, or being guaranteed true in the relevant sense.
The view that certainty consists in justification of the highest degree. The entry examines difficulties in specifying “highest.”
The view that certainty requires immunity from both relevant subjective and objective defeaters. The entry argues that this proposal faces serious problems.
Certainty at a particular time, contrasted with certainty that remains secure across changes in evidence and belief.
Certainty understood as stable within an interconnected system of beliefs over an extended period.

questions_to_think_about: If a person has the strongest confidence for irrational reasons, is the belief psychologically certain, epistemically certain, both, or neither?
What would make a belief immune to doubt for the right reasons rather than merely impossible for someone to question?
Can a necessary truth be believed in a way that is not epistemically certain?
Should a person assert a claim only when certain, or is knowledge that falls short of certainty enough?
Does certainty need to remain stable when new evidence appears, or can momentary certainty be genuine?

summaries.example: A weather app says there is a 95% chance of rain, so you bring an umbrella. You are not completely certain that it will rain, but your evidence is strong enough for the choice. Now imagine that you personally feel 100% sure because you always trust the app, even though you have not checked whether it is working. Your confidence is psychological certainty. The strong evidence might support a high level of knowledge, but it may still fall short of philosophical certainty.
summaries.summary: Certainty concerns the status of a belief, but the entry separates several ideas that are often mixed together. Psychological certainty is a person’s strongest conviction. Epistemic certainty is a belief’s highest possible epistemic standing—its strongest relation to truth, evidence, or justification. A person can feel certain for weak reasons, and a belief could have excellent support without its holder realizing how good that support is. The entry describes four main approaches to epistemic certainty. On an indubitability view, a certain belief cannot be doubted, but being unable to doubt may come from habit or irrational commitment. On an infallibility view, a certain belief cannot be false, though philosophers must explain what kind of possibility is being ruled out. On an inimitability view, certainty is the highest degree of justification, but it is difficult to say whether this means highest for one person, for everyone, or in principle. On an indefeasibility view, no appropriate new reason could lower the belief’s support, yet it is difficult to explain how beliefs defeat one another and how merely removing possible defeaters would create certainty. The entry also distinguishes certainty at a particular time from certainty that lasts and fits into a complete system of beliefs. Finally, it considers whether certainty should be required for making claims or for using beliefs in decisions. Skeptics emphasize how hard certainty may be to achieve; other philosophers defend useful forms of knowledge and reasoning below that level.
key_ideas: A person’s confidence and a belief’s evidential support are different things, so psychological and epistemic certainty can come apart.
Philosophers disagree about whether certainty is the same as knowledge or a stronger status than knowledge. Some allow fallible knowledge: knowledge that could have been mistaken.
Four important proposals describe certainty as freedom from doubt, freedom from error, the highest justification, or resistance to defeating evidence.
The word “highest” creates problems. It might mean highest for one person, highest among actual people, or the highest level that is possible, and these options have different consequences.
Certainty can be temporary or durable. A belief may be secure while someone is directly considering it but lose that security later, or it may be supported by a stable system of beliefs.
Some philosophers propose certainty as the standard for proper assertion or practical reliance. Others argue that ordinary life often requires acting on very good but uncertain beliefs.
summaries.why_it_matters: Everyday decisions rarely come with perfect guarantees, but people still need to judge when evidence is strong enough. Studying certainty helps us notice the difference between confidence, truth, knowledge, and justification. It also explains why a skeptical challenge might show that certainty is rare without showing that all less-than-certain beliefs are worthless.

important_terms.definition: Belief with the highest possible epistemic status, meaning the best kind of support or justification in the relevant sense.
Being extremely convinced that a claim is true. This describes a person’s mental confidence, not necessarily the quality of the evidence.
The philosophical position that challenges whether people can have certainty, or sometimes even knowledge, because doubts can always be raised.
The view that a certain belief could not have been mistaken or false in the relevant sense.
The view that a belief is justified as strongly as possible, rather than merely being the best-supported belief a particular person happens to have.
The view that a belief cannot be undermined by suitable new evidence or reasons for doubt.
A kind of certainty that is good enough to guide ordinary behavior, even though it may not be absolute certainty.
The idea that what counts as certain can change with the conversational or practical situation.

questions_to_think_about: Would a person’s belief be certain if they were fully confident but had no good evidence?
Can you know something without being certain of it? What would that difference be?
Is “good enough for everyday life” a genuine kind of certainty or a different kind of rational support?
Should the standards for certainty change when the consequences of being wrong become more serious?
When you rely on a likely claim, are you really relying on that claim or on the claim that it is likely?
